slides.0.title: Viticulture in Depth and Climate Change
slides.0.subtitle: Northern and southern challenges and adaptation
slides.1.title: Northern Rhône: steep slopes, hand work and hillside economics
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Extremely steep slopes
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Côte-Rôtie's steepest parcels: the growers' ODG gives 60% inclination while Inter Rhône says 'over 60°' in places. The units differ, so remember only 'extremely steep'; the figure is not examined
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Terraces and dry-stone walls
slides.1.highlights.1.content: On the Côte Blonde the crumbly sandy clay (arzel) cannot be farmed without dry-stone walls (cheys); the Côte Brune has narrow terraces (chaillées) (WineWithSeth)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Compulsory hand harvest and high density
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Côte-Rôtie must be hand-harvested; at least 6,000 vines per hectare with rows no wider than 2 m; training may be gobelet, cordon de Royat or single Guyot, pruned to at most 10 buds per vine
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Stake training (échalas)
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Traditionally each vine is tied to its own stake to resist wind on steep ground; wires are now common too. This is a general account and varies by appellation and estate
slides.1.highlights.4.title: Hillside economics
slides.1.highlights.4.content: High labour, little mechanisation and low yields (Côte-Rôtie specification: 40 hl/ha) mean the model depends on high prices and scarcity; when prices fail, terraces are abandoned
slides.1.content: Essay skeleton: slope → hand labour, hard to mechanise → high cost, low yield → sustained by high prices and scarcity; the failure mode is abandoned terraces.
slides.2.title: Southern Rhône: old-vine Grenache, drought and the Mistral
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Old bush vines (gobelet)
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Low, free-standing, mostly dry-farmed old Grenache vines shade the bunches and root deeply — the traditional southern answer to heat and wind; old vines give low yields and concentration (general account)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The Mistral
slides.2.highlights.1.content: WineWithSeth says the Mistral blows about 120 days a year with over 2,500 sunshine hours (single source, not examined). It dries the grapes and reduces fungal disease, but also breaks shoots, hampers pollination and worsens water stress
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Rainfall pattern
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Summers are hot and dry and rain falls mainly in autumn and late winter (WineWithSeth); violent storms can cause erosion and flooding, so drought and downpours coexist
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Frost, hail and vintage swings
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Spring frost and hail make yields swing: the valley averaged about 33 hl/ha in 2025 (Inter Rhône), Côtes du Rhône averaged 41 hl/ha in 2021 against a 51 hl/ha specification (wein.plus; INAO draft)
slides.2.highlights.4.title: Stones and water retention
slides.2.highlights.4.content: Châteauneuf's rolled pebbles (galets roulés) store daytime heat, release it at night and reduce evaporation (general account); differences in water retention between sand, clay and limestone decide which plots cope best in dry years
slides.2.content: Essay skeleton: wind → low gobelet training; drought → old vines, dry farming, low yield; frost and hail → vintage volatility, so spread risk across varieties and plots.
slides.3.title: Climate change: what the data say
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Earlier phenology
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The Institut rhodanien tracked Grenache ripening since 1969 (BKWine Magazine, 2022): budburst and flowering are 10–15 days earlier and harvest often starts about 20 days earlier
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Rising potential alcohol
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Before 1990 about 12.5% at harvest (about 10% on 1 September); now often over 14% at harvest (about 12.5% in early September); in 2019 and 2020 it exceeded 15% by mid-September
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Lower acidity, smaller berries
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Total acidity fell by about 1.95 g/L; 200 berries weighed 380–400 g in 2000 and 280 g in 2019, which means lower yields
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Causes and caveats
slides.3.highlights.3.content: The researchers link the changes to higher temperatures between flowering and véraison and fewer days with relative humidity above 60%, while acknowledging that part of the earlier timing comes from better vineyard knowledge, not climate alone
slides.3.highlights.4.title: Stylistic consequences
slides.3.highlights.4.content: Côtes du Rhône reds commonly run 13–14.5% abv (WineWithSeth). Higher alcohol, lower acidity and sugar ripeness decoupled from phenolic ripeness make harvest timing and whole-cluster or destemming choices more critical
slides.3.content: These figures come from one study reported second-hand, so they are sourced here and not examined; for the exam keep the direction: earlier, more sugar, less acid, smaller berries, lower yields.
slides.4.title: Adaptation: varieties, viticulture and sustainability
slides.4.highlights.0.title: VIFA adaptation varieties
slides.4.highlights.0.content: VIFA on trial in Côtes du Rhône and Villages: white Carignan blanc, Floréal and Rolle (Vermentino), red Vidoc (Inter Rhône glossary, April 2025)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Two different caps
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Each estate may use at most 5% of its vineyard area and 10% of the final blend; the observation period is 10 years, after which the appellation decides. Sources quoting only 10% or only 5% are describing two different limits
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Disease-resistant varieties
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Floréal and Vidoc (and Souvignier gris in Costières de Nîmes) are tested for resistance to downy and powdery mildew, which can cut spraying; Costières de Nîmes has its own VIFA list
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Organic and HVE
slides.4.highlights.3.content: 2025 harvest: organic about 26% of area and 24% of volume (cover chart says 25%); HVE3 about 34% of area and 37% of volume (Inter Rhône Chiffres clés 2025). Approximate figures, not examined
slides.4.highlights.4.title: Other levers
slides.4.highlights.4.content: Higher or north-facing sites, cover crops and canopy management, later pruning; wein.plus also reports heat- and drought-tolerant white varieties such as Picpoul and Bourboulenc as suitable (some levers are general accounts)
slides.4.content: Essay skeleton: state the risks (heat, drought, rising alcohol), then the responses (varieties, viticulture, sustainability), then the trade-off between traditional style and AOC variety rules versus adaptation.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Which describes Côte-Rôtie's viticultural and harvest rules?
A. Machine harvest allowed, about 2,500 vines per hectare
B. Hand harvest compulsory, at least 6,000 vines per hectare
C. Machine harvest compulsory to cut costs
D. No viticultural rules at all
Côte-Rôtie must be hand-harvested and requires high planting density (at least 6,000 vines per hectare).
What are the VIFA trial limits for each Côtes du Rhône estate?
A. 1% of area and 2% of the blend
B. 20% of area and 50% of the blend
C. 5% of area and 10% of the blend
D. No limit
At most 5% of area and 10% of the blend, with a 10-year observation period.
Which describes the direction of change in southern Rhône Grenache ripening over recent decades?
A. Earlier harvest, higher potential alcohol, lower acidity
B. Later harvest, lower alcohol, higher acidity
C. Earlier harvest, lower alcohol, higher acidity
D. No change in any of these
The Institut rhodanien study shows earlier phenology, more sugar and lower total acidity (specific figures are indicative only).
Which is the only red variety among the Côtes du Rhône VIFA trial varieties?
A. Rolle
B. Floréal
C. Carignan blanc
D. Vidoc
Vidoc is red; Rolle, Floréal and Carignan blanc are white.
